settings.title: Settings
settings.reckoningHelp: There is no single correct calendar. Choose the one your practice or kindred follows.

reckoningDescription.solar: Tides fall on the solstices, equinoxes and the days midway between them. The most common modern approach.
reckoningDescription.lunar: Each tide falls on the full moon after its seasonal marker. A modern reconstruction; some scholars argue pre-Christian feasts followed the moon, and details vary between groups.
reckoningDescription.icelandic: Uses the weekday rules of the medieval Icelandic calendar (misseristal): the first day of summer, the first day of winter, and the months Þorri and Góa.

settings.hemisphereHelp: In the southern hemisphere the Wheel turns with your seasons, so Yule falls in June.
settings.valuesBody: Hearth & Well is for everyone who is called to the gods, ancestors and wights of the North, whatever their ancestry, ethnicity, gender or sexuality. There is no place here for racism or for using the tradition to exclude people.
settings.freeBody: The gods, the sources and the practice will never be behind a paywall. No ads, and your data is never sold.
settings.readerLanguageHelp: Show the English translation, the Old Norse original, or both together.

yule.name: Yule
yule.summary: Midwinter: the longest nights, the return of the sun, and the holiest tide of the year.
yule.about: Yule (Jól) is the great midwinter feast. Heimskringla says that before King Hákon the Good moved it to coincide with Christmas, Yule began on hǫkunótt, "midwinter night", and was kept for three nights. Feasting, drinking toasts to the gods and swearing oaths were at its heart. Today many Heathens keep twelve nights, beginning with Mother's Night in honour of the dísir and ancestral mothers.
yule.observance: Light a candle or fire at nightfall on Mother's Night and name the women of your line. Hold a feast and a sumbel with toasts to the gods, the ancestors and your living kin. Make a Yule oath for the year to come, and keep it.

sources.hokunott: King Hákon made a law moving the start of Yule to the Christian date; before that it began on hǫkunótt (midwinter night) and lasted three nights.
sources.hladir: Describes a sacrificial feast at Hlaðir, with toasts to Óðinn for victory and to Njǫrðr and Freyr for good seasons and peace.
sources.modranecht: Bede records that the pagan English began their year on 25 December, calling that night Modranecht, "night of the mothers".
sources.twelveNights: Most modern Heathens keep twelve nights of Yule, usually starting on Mother's Night, the eve of the solstice.

prep.candles: Gather candles or wood for a Yule fire
prep.mothersNight: Learn the names of the mothers in your line for Mother's Night
prep.oath: Think carefully about an oath you can keep for the coming year
prep.feast: Plan the Yule feast and who you will share it with

thorrablot.name: Þorrablót
thorrablot.summary: A midwinter feast at the start of the old Icelandic month Þorri.
thorrablot.about: Þorri is a month of the Old Icelandic calendar, beginning in late January. A legendary account says a king named Þorri held a sacrifice every midwinter that was called Þorrablót, and the month took its name from him. The feast was revived in 19th-century Iceland and is now celebrated across Iceland and by Heathens worldwide with traditional food, drink and song.
thorrablot.observance: Share a hearty winter meal with friends and family. Raise a horn to Þorri and to the gods, and tell stories through the long evening.

sources.thorri: Tells of Þorri, who held a sacrifice every year at midwinter called Þorrablót; the month Þorri was named after him.
sources.revival: Þorrablót feasts were revived in Iceland in the 19th century and remain a popular midwinter tradition.

prep.food: Plan a winter feast; traditional Icelandic dishes are optional
prep.guests: Invite friends, family or your kindred
prep.toast: Prepare a toast or a story to share

disablot.name: Dísablót
disablot.summary: An offering to the dísir: protective female spirits and ancestral mothers.
disablot.about: The dísir are female powers who watch over families and individuals, often understood as ancestral mothers. Sources show dísablót being held at different times in different places: in Sweden it was tied to the great Uppsala assembly in late winter, while Icelandic sagas place it at Winter Nights in autumn. In this app, Dísablót marks the late-winter observance; the autumn one is part of Winter Nights.
disablot.observance: Set out an offering of food and drink for the dísir. Speak the names of the women in your family who have died, and ask the dísir to keep watch over your household.

sources.uppsala: The chief sacrifice of the Swedes was held at Uppsala in the month Gói, together with an assembly and market (the Dísaþing).
sources.adils: King Aðils dies after his horse stumbles while he rides around the hall of the dísir during a dísablót.
sources.autumn: A dísablót is held at Winter Nights, showing that in Iceland it could be an autumn observance.
sources.modern: Many modern Heathens honour the dísir in late winter; others do so at Winter Nights.

prep.names: Write down the names of the women in your line you wish to honour
prep.offering: Prepare food and drink for the offering

sigrblot.name: Sigrblót
sigrblot.summary: The summer sacrifice "for victory", welcoming the light half of the year.
sigrblot.about: Snorri Sturluson writes that Óðinn established three great sacrifices: at the beginning of winter for a good year, at midwinter for growth, and at summer for victory (sigr). Sigrblót celebrates the arrival of summer and asks for success in the season's undertakings. The Old Icelandic calendar's first day of summer, still a public holiday in Iceland, falls in late April. Many modern Heathens call this tide Summer Finding.
sigrblot.observance: Make an offering to Óðinn or the gods you honour and name what you hope to achieve this summer. Spend time outdoors and greet the returning season.

sources.odinsLaw: Óðinn's law: sacrifice at the beginning of winter for a good year, at midwinter for growth, and at summer for victory.
sources.firstDayOfSummer: The first day of summer falls on the Thursday between 19 and 25 April. It is still a public holiday in Iceland.
sources.summerFinding: Many modern calendars celebrate "Summer Finding" at the spring equinox or in mid-April.

prep.goal: Choose a goal for the summer to dedicate
prep.outdoors: Find an outdoor place for the blót
prep.offering: Prepare an offering of mead, ale or juice

midsummer.name: Midsummer
midsummer.summary: The height of the sun: bonfires, flowers and the shortest night.
midsummer.about: Midsummer remains one of the most beloved festivals in the Nordic countries, with bonfires, flower garlands and dancing. Its pre-Christian roots are likely but thinly recorded in Old Norse sources, so much of what we know comes from later folk custom. Modern Heathens celebrate the sun at its height and the bounty of the season.
midsummer.observance: Light a fire, gather flowers, and stay up through the shortest night. Give thanks to Sól, the sun, and to the gods of growth and plenty.

sources.folk: Midsummer bonfires and celebrations are well documented in Scandinavian folk custom from later centuries.
sources.modern: Modern Heathens widely celebrate Midsummer at the summer solstice.

prep.fire: Plan a safe fire or candles
prep.flowers: Gather flowers for a garland or the altar
prep.sunrise: Check the times of sunset and sunrise

freyfaxi.name: Freyfaxi
freyfaxi.summary: A modern harvest festival honouring Freyr and the first fruits.
freyfaxi.about: Freyfaxi takes its name from the stallion in Hrafnkels saga that the chieftain Hrafnkell dedicated to Freyr. The festival itself is modern: Heathens celebrate the first harvest, give thanks to Freyr for the fertility of the land, and often hold games and contests.
freyfaxi.observance: Bake bread from new grain, offer the first fruits of your garden or market, and give thanks to Freyr and the land.

sources.horse: Hrafnkell dedicates his horse Freyfaxi to Freyr and swears to kill anyone who rides it without his leave.
sources.harvest: A modern Heathen first-harvest festival, usually held in early August in the northern hemisphere.

prep.firstFruits: Set aside the first fruits of the season
prep.bread: Bake or buy a loaf of fresh bread
prep.thanks: Think of what the land has given you this year

haustblot.name: Haustblót
haustblot.summary: Autumn thanksgiving at the equinox, as the days and nights become equal.
haustblot.about: Haustblót ("autumn sacrifice") is a modern name for a harvest thanksgiving at the autumn equinox. It is a time to give thanks for the year's harvest, share abundance, and honour the land-wights who make it possible.
haustblot.observance: Share a harvest meal, give part of it back to the land as an offering to the landvættir, and give to those in need.

sources.harvest: A modern Heathen harvest festival at the autumn equinox.

prep.harvest: Gather seasonal food for a harvest meal
prep.share: Choose a way to share with those in need
prep.landwights: Find a place outdoors to leave an offering to the land-wights

winterNights.name: Winter Nights
winterNights.summary: The turning of the year toward winter: a time for the ancestors, the álfar and the dísir.
winterNights.about: Winter Nights (Vetrnætr) mark the start of winter in the Old Icelandic calendar. Snorri names a sacrifice "at the beginning of winter, for a good year", and the sagas place a dísablót at Winter Nights. The skald Sigvatr tells of being turned away from a Swedish farm during an álfablót, an offering to the elves, in autumn. Many Heathens consider Winter Nights the start of the new year.
winterNights.observance: Honour your ancestors, the álfar and the dísir with a quiet household blót. Take stock of the year's harvest and your stores for winter.

sources.odinsLaw: Óðinn's law: sacrifice at the beginning of winter for a good year.
sources.disablot: A dísablót is held at Winter Nights.
sources.alfablot: Sigvatr is refused hospitality at farms in Sweden because an álfablót is being held.
sources.firstDayOfWinter: The first day of winter falls on the Saturday between 21 and 27 October.

prep.ancestors: Gather photos or mementos of your ancestors
prep.alfar: Prepare a private offering for the álfar
prep.stores: Take stock of what you have for the winter ahead

prompts.havamal-1: Where in your life are you walking through a new door? What would it mean to enter it with open eyes?
prompts.havamal-3: Who in your life has come in from the cold lately? What could you offer them?
prompts.havamal-4: How do you welcome people into your home or your day? What would make that welcome warmer?
prompts.havamal-6: When did you last keep your cleverness to yourself, and what did you learn by listening instead?
prompts.havamal-7: In your next conversation, try simply to listen and watch. What do you notice that you usually miss?
prompts.havamal-10: What wisdom do you carry that has helped you through hard times? Where did it come from?
prompts.havamal-15: What would it look like to meet today bravely and gladly, whatever it brings?
prompts.havamal-19: Where could more measure (in drink, in words, in effort) serve you well today?
prompts.havamal-22: What fault in yourself have you been slow to see? How might you begin to mend it?
prompts.havamal-23: What worry has kept you awake? Does the morning change it, or only your mood?
prompts.havamal-28: What question could you ask someone today that would teach you something real?
prompts.havamal-34: Which friend is far away but close in heart? How could you reach them this week?
prompts.havamal-36: What do you have, however small, that is truly your own? How can you give thanks for it?
prompts.havamal-41: What gift, of time, help or a thing made by hand, could you give a friend this week?
prompts.havamal-42: Is there a gift you have received but not yet answered? How might you return it?
prompts.havamal-44: Who do you trust fully? When did you last go to see them?
prompts.havamal-47: Think of a time a companion made a lonely road easier. Who might need that from you now?
prompts.havamal-50: Who around you may feel unloved or alone? What small thing could you do for them?
prompts.havamal-52: Small kindnesses make lasting friends. What half-loaf could you share today?
prompts.havamal-53: Where are you tempted to think you have the whole truth? What might you still not know?
prompts.havamal-56: What would change if you stopped trying to see what is coming, and lived today well?
prompts.havamal-57: Whose words have kindled something in you? What fire could your words light for someone else?
prompts.havamal-59: What task have you been putting off that would be half done if you simply began?
prompts.havamal-61: Where are you holding back for fear of not looking good enough? What if you went anyway?
prompts.havamal-63: Who is the one person you can tell your thoughts to? What would you like to tell them?
prompts.havamal-68: Fire, sunlight, health and a clean life: which of these gifts are you most thankful for today?
prompts.havamal-69: On a hard day, where do you still find joy: in kin, in work, in what you have?
prompts.havamal-72: Who among your ancestors deserves remembering? How could you honour them?
prompts.havamal-75: Who have you been quick to look down on? What would it take to set that scorn aside?
prompts.havamal-77: What do you want to be remembered for? What did you do today toward it?
prompts.havamal-81: What are you judging too early? What would it mean to wait and see how it turns out?
prompts.havamal-89: Where are you counting on a harvest before the season has turned? How can you tend it patiently?
prompts.havamal-95: What is close to your heart that no one else knows? How are you caring for it?
prompts.havamal-103: How can you be both joyful and wise in company today?
prompts.havamal-111: Óðinn saw, was silent, and thought. Spend a few minutes in silence today. What comes to you?
prompts.havamal-119: Which friendship is becoming an overgrown path? What could you do to walk it again?
prompts.havamal-121: Is there something you have been carrying alone that you could share with a friend?
prompts.havamal-124: Who can you speak to honestly, without pretending? How do you keep that friendship true?
prompts.havamal-131: Where is caution serving you, and where has it turned into fear?
prompts.havamal-133: Think of someone you find difficult. What good can you see in them?
prompts.havamal-134: What has an older person taught you that you still carry? Who could you ask for counsel now?
prompts.havamal-135: Who in your community is in want? What could you do for them this week?
prompts.havamal-139: Óðinn gave himself to himself to win the runes. What would you be willing to give for wisdom?
prompts.havamal-142: What small deed today could lead to another good deed, and another?
prompts.havamal-146: What offering is right for you to give, not too great and not too small? How does a gift call for a gift?
prompts.voluspa-18: Breath, sense, warmth and colour were gifts of the gods. How can you honour the life you were given?
prompts.voluspa-19: Yggdrasil is kept green by the well at its root. What keeps you green and growing?
prompts.voluspa-20: The Norns shape what is. What in your life is already laid down, and what is still being shaped by you?
prompts.voluspa-59: After the end, the earth rises green again. What in your life is ready to begin anew?

runes.title: Runes
runes.intro: The Younger Futhark was the runic script of the Viking Age, the world the Eddas remember. Its sixteen runes are the only ones the Norse rune poems describe. The Eddas themselves were never written in runes: they survive in the Latin alphabet, in Icelandic manuscripts of the 13th century.
runes.youngerAbout: The meanings come from the Norwegian rune poem (13th century) and the Icelandic rune poem (15th century), both written down in Christian times.
runes.elderAbout: No Norse poem describes these runes. Their names are reconstructed from the later Norse, Anglo-Saxon and Gothic rune names, so they are marked with an asterisk.
runes.styleHelp: Long-branch runes were usual in Denmark; short-twig runes, quicker to carve, in Sweden and Norway.
runes.meaningUncertain: The meaning of this name is uncertain.
runes.glossHelp: Each Icelandic stanza ends with a Latin translation of the rune’s name and an alliterating word for “king”.
runes.ancestor: Descends from the Elder Futhark rune {{name}}
runes.descendant: Continues in the Younger Futhark as {{name}}
runes.writtenWith: Dropped from the Younger Futhark. Its sound was then written with {{name}}.
runes.reflectNote: Our own words, inspired by the poems. Not a traditional meaning.
runes.modernNote: Modern esoteric and divinatory meanings are not ancient; when we add them they will be clearly labelled.

draw.title: Today’s rune
draw.prompt: Draw one rune to reflect on today. This is for contemplation, not fortune-telling.
draw.again: A new rune can be drawn tomorrow.

fe.prompt: Both poems call wealth a source of strife among kin. Where does what you have draw people together, and where does it set them apart?

ur.prompt: Dross comes from bad iron, yet the reindeer runs over the frozen snow. What hardship has shown you what you are made of?

thurs.prompt: The giant brings torment, and misfortune cheers few. What overwhelming force are you facing, and who could stand beside you?

oss.prompt: The god is aged Gautr: Óðinn, lord of Valhalla, who gave much for wisdom. What are you willing to give to understand more?

reid.prompt: Riding is joy for the rider and toil for the horse. Whose effort carries you forward, and how do you repay it?

kaun.prompt: A sore drains the colour from a face. What wound, in body or heart, needs your care instead of your neglect?

hagall.prompt: Hail is the coldest of grain, yet it falls on the growing fields. What has come to you hard that may still feed you?

naudr.prompt: Need leaves little choice. When your options are few, what do you choose to hold on to?

iss.prompt: Ice is a broad bridge, but the blind must be led across. Where are you standing on something that may not hold, and who could guide you?

ar.prompt: Plenty is a boon to all, and Fróði was generous. How could you share the good your year has brought?

sol.prompt: The sun is the light of the lands and the destroyer of ice. What warms you, and whom could you warm today?

tyr.prompt: Týr gave his hand so the wolf could be bound. What have you given up, or would you give up, to keep faith with others?

bjarkan.prompt: The birch is small, leafy and young. What is new and growing in your life that needs tending?

madr.prompt: "Man is the delight of man," as the Hávamál also says. Whose company delights you, and do they know it?

logr.prompt: Water falls from the mountain and the cauldron boils over. What is moving in you that needs an outlet?

yr.prompt: The yew stays green in winter and bends into a bow. Where do you need to bend without breaking?

ansuz.meaning: a god, one of the Æsir
